analysis.one_liner: Bars bank regulators from pressuring banks to drop legally operating business customers and weakens the Justice Department's subpoena power over financial institutions.
analysis.headline: The bill, meant to stop regulators from pressuring banks to cut off disfavored businesses, never got a committee vote and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After federal regulators targeted banks that served certain disfavored-but-legal businesses under what critics called "Operation Choke Point," this bill would have made it illegal for banking regulators to prohibit, restrict, or even "discourage" banks from serving any business that is licensed, registered as a money transmitter, or backed by a lawyer's written opinion that its business is legal. It would also have repealed the Justice Department's administrative subpoena power over financial fraud cases, forcing prosecutors to get a court order instead. The bill died in the House Financial Services Committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses in industries regulators consider high-risk — notably payday lenders, firearms dealers, and other payment-dependent firms — would gain a near-guaranteed right to banking services as long as they hold a license, a money-transmitter registration, or a written legal opinion. Banks and credit unions also gain: they could not be penalized for serving those customers, and they would gain immunity for the underlying activity they report, plus protection from DOJ's administrative subpoenas in financial-fraud investigations.

how_it_helps.text: Bars federal banking regulators from prohibiting, restricting, or discouraging banks from providing products or services to businesses that are licensed, registered as money transmitters, or backed by a lawyer's written opinion that the business is legal.
Repeals the Attorney General's administrative subpoena power under FIRREA, requiring a court order supported by specific facts before financial records can be compelled in a fraud investigation.

Narrows the USA PATRIOT Act's bank information-sharing program so shared information cannot be used for purposes beyond identifying fraud, terrorism, or money laundering, and extends banks' legal immunity to the underlying activity they disclose.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and honest businesses bear the cost of weaker fraud enforcement: easier payment access for fraud-heavy industries means more scams reaching the public, and the repeal of DOJ's administrative subpoena power slows investigations into bank and payment fraud. Legitimate small businesses in disfavored industries that genuinely need banking would lose out on the relief the bill promised.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers facing more fraud and scams

drawbacks.text: By barring regulators from discouraging banks from serving any licensed entity or one with a lawyer's opinion that its business is legal, the bill would remove a key tool regulators and the Justice Department had used to cut off access to payment processing for fraud-heavy industries, costs that fall on consumers.
Repealing the Attorney General's administrative subpoena authority under FIRREA and requiring a court order would slow federal investigations into financial fraud at banks and businesses.

Extending legal immunity to banks for the 'underlying activity' they report, and barring regulators from requiring banks to verify licensing compliance, would shift the risk of doing business with questionable operators onto the public and away from the banks that profit from those accounts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The concerns behind the bill were real: some lawful businesses were being cut off from banks through pressure campaigns rather than case-by-case risk decisions, and a subpoena process with no judicial check deserves scrutiny. But the remedy went much further than fixing those problems. Barring regulators from even "discouraging" bank relationships with legally licensed businesses would make it far harder to police fraud-prone industries that ordinary consumers bear the cost of, and stripping the Justice Department's administrative subpoena power in financial-fraud cases would slow investigations. A narrower bill addressing specific due-process objections would have been a more honest trade.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and died there without ever being voted on.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 26, 2014 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee the same day.
The Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit held a hearing on July 15, 2014, but the full committee never voted to send the bill to the House floor.
No further action was taken before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, so the bill received no floor vote and died.
It had 14 cosponsors, 11 Republicans and 3 Democrats, but never attracted the broader support or committee approval needed to reach a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, regulators and the Justice Department kept their ability to pressure banks away from fraud-prone industries and to subpoena records without a court order, tools that protect consumers from financial fraud. Banks and high-risk businesses seeking guaranteed access to the banking system did not get the new protections.

for.name: Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer

for.name: Community banking industry groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly opposed Operation Choke Point and backed legislation to restrict regulators from pressuring banks over customer accounts.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee vote after a July 15, 2014 subcommittee hearing, keeping it off the House floor.

against.name: 113th House of Representatives
against.what_they_did: Never voted on the bill before the Congress ended January 3, 2015.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided, 11 Republicans to 3 Democrats, and the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would show the real party split.

industries.industry: High-risk payment-dependent businesses (payday lenders, firearms dealers, etc.)
industries.note: The bill would guarantee these businesses access to the banking system even when regulators conclude their industries are rife with fraud. Ordinary consumers pay through higher fraud losses and easier access to predatory loans.

Regulators could no longer discourage or restrict banking relationships, and banks would gain immunity even for the underlying activity they report to regulators. This reduces their compliance and legal exposure at some cost to fraud enforcement.

DOJ would lose its administrative subpoena power in financial-fraud cases and its informal channel of asking banks to cut off fraudulent operators, slowing investigations that protect consumers' money.
